opal-0084: You can hold my hand. If you don't mind it being a bit... wet.
opal-0085: We're getting the second owl, right?
opal-0086: Obviously we're getting the second owl.
opal-0087: They're a pair. I'm not splitting up a pair.
opal-0088: Four hundred and twelve buttons, twenty-six keys, a glass eye and two owls. The alchemist's men are felling the north woods now, so Opal is staying with you, and her collection takes up a whole shelf in your front room. She rearranges it twice.
opal-0089: It's all here. All of it. I counted three times.
opal-0090: Her jar sits at the end of the shelf with the lid off. She hasn't been in it for three days.
opal-0091: I have to tell you something. I kept something of yours. On the first day.

opal-0093: It's the first thing in a new collection. Things that are yours.
opal-0094: C-can I sleep in your room tonight? Not in the jar. With you.
opal-0095: Turn the lamp down a bit? Everything shows, with me.

opal-0098: Oh. I didn't know I did that. That's embarrassing. Do it again.
opal-0099: I should tell you I don't know what I'm doing. I've only heard about this. Through glass. People say a lot on a forest path when they think no one's listening.
opal-0100: Mostly couples who thought they'd found somewhere private. So I know a lot about not lying down in nettles.
opal-0101: You laugh. She goes pink all the way through, and then she laughs too.
opal-0102: She takes your hand and presses it gently against her. It sinks in a little, cool and soft, and she shivers.
opal-0103: I-is that all right? Tell me if it's strange. You can say it's strange.
opal-0104: You tell her it isn't strange. She pulls you closer, and for once she doesn't apologise for anything.
opal-0105: Afterwards she's spread across most of the bed and some of you, glowing faintly, humming something Ambrose used to whistle.
opal-0106: There are four hundred and forty-one things in my collection. I'm trying to work out how to write a card for tonight.
opal-0107: It's going to need a very long card.
opal-0108: Th-thank you. Sorry. No. Not sorry. Thank you.
opal-0109: The jar stays empty all night.
opal-0111: Opal moves in properly. Her collection grows a second shelf, then a third: things you've dropped, things your friends have dropped, the ticket from your first evening out together. The jar lives under the bed. She uses it twice that year, both times in thunderstorms, and both times you sit on the floor beside it while she tells you, through the glass, which of the neighbours owe each other money. She climbs out on her own before the storm is over.
opal-0112: Something cool and slightly heavy is draped over you like a blanket. It turns out to be her.
opal-0113: Sorry. I spread out in my sleep. I didn't know that. I've never slept anywhere big enough to find out.
opal-0114: Last night was the best thing that's happened to me in thirty-one years. Possibly ever. I'm not exaggerating. I've had a lot of time to compare.
opal-0115: I'd like to do it again. That's allowed to be said, isn't it? Good. I'd like to do it again.
opal-0116: I've started a card for last night. For the collection. I'm on my fourth draft.
opal-0117: Morning light through the bedroom curtains, and someone translucent and lilac curled over the covers.
opal-0118: She goes outside on her own for the first time to buy bread. She's gone twenty minutes. You both pretend you weren't worried.
opal-0119: The baker asked my name. I told him. Then I told him about buttons for a while. He was very patient.
opal-0120: I'm going back tomorrow. He does a seeded loaf on Thursdays.
opal-0121: Opal at the baker's counter, a loaf under one arm and a stray button in her hand.
opal-0122: The jar. Should I keep it? I haven't been in it for a week. I still check it's there.
opal-0123: You tell her to keep it. For storms.
opal-0124: For storms. Okay. Just for storms.
hazel-0005: Mm. That one smells like April.
hazel-0012: No. I've seen what those do.
hazel-0013: Embers. I'll pretend I didn't see that.
hazel-0015: Slower. I can hear you panicking.
hazel-0016: Forty years, I said. Mind where you swing.
hazel-0017: The ferns are watching. Give them something to talk about.
hazel-0018: You've got mud on your face. Leave it. It suits you.
hazel-0019: Better than the last one Aldous sent. Prettier, too.
hazel-0020: I'm not watching you. I'm photosynthesising.
hazel-0021: Take your time. I've got a few hundred years.
hazel-0022: If you see the miller, wave. It makes him nervous.
hazel-0023: The badgers think you're doing well. They're wrong, but it's sweet.
hazel-0025: A folding brass sundial small enough for a pocket. It only tells the time on sunny days, which as far as she's concerned are the only days that need it.
hazel-0026: She makes you hold it up in the one patch of sun that gets through her leaves, and watches the shadow for a long time.
hazel-0027: A clock that only works when the sun's out. Someone finally made one that keeps sensible hours.
hazel-0028: The green at the tips of her hair goes a shade darker. She notices, and decides not to mention it.
hazel-0029: I'll hang it on the low branch. You can see the path from there, which is where you come from. Not that I watch it.
hazel-0030: The old hazel stands where the grove meets the millrace. It's so big that the mill's back wall has started to bend round its roots.
hazel-0031: You're new in town and you'll take any work that pays. The miller paid you half up front to cut the tree down. You pick a spot on the trunk that looks right, plant your feet and lift the axe.
hazel-0033: There's a woman sitting on the lowest branch, where you're sure nobody was a second ago. Her hair goes from gold to green, and below the knee her legs turn into bark.
hazel-0034: She looks at the axe, then at the place on the trunk you were aiming for.
hazel-0035: You were aiming just below my heart. That takes forty years or so to heal.
hazel-0036: Let me guess. Aldous paid you half up front.
hazel-0037: You lower the axe. After a moment, you put it down on the grass.
hazel-0038: Oh. You're putting it down. Most of them argue first.
hazel-0039: The last one argued with the axe still in his hands, so I dropped a beehive on him. I wouldn't do that to you. Your face is too nice to waste on bees.
hazel-0040: You tell her about the wall. Her roots are cracking it, and when it goes, the miller loses his mill.
hazel-0041: I know about the wall. My roots go where the water is, and they've never once asked my opinion.
hazel-0042: If someone dug him a new channel further out, my roots would follow the water. It would take a season. Nobody's ever offered. It's a lot of digging.
hazel-0043: I'll dig it. Show me where.
hazel-0044: By hand? You'll be at it till midsummer. I suppose I'll have to put up with you all spring.
hazel-0045: A leaf drops into your hair. There's no wind.
hazel-0046: Start by the alder, the ground's soft there. And roll your sleeves up. For the digging.
hazel-0047: I'll dig. I'm keeping the miller's money, though.
hazel-0048: Keep it. Buy yourself a better axe and never use it.
hazel-0049: Start by the alder. If you hit a root, say sorry. It's me, and I'll be listening.
hazel-0050: You dig until sunset. The trench ends up about the length of a coffin, which she points out twice.
hazel-0051: That's a lovely trench, if you're planning to bury somebody. For a millrace it's a start.
hazel-0052: When you climb out you lean on the trunk to get your breath back. The bark is rough and cool under your hand.
hazel-0053: Oh. You're warm. Nobody's put a hand on me in years, unless they were measuring where to cut.
hazel-0054: You start to take your hand away. She says you don't have to.
hazel-0055: Leave it. Bit lower, if you like. The bark's softer.
hazel-0056: How long have you been out here on your own?
hazel-0057: Since the grove was a forest. Two hundred years, give or take a drought.
hazel-0058: The badgers visit. They don't talk much, and none of them has ever leaned on me like that.
hazel-0059: If I'd known you liked it, I'd have come by sooner.
hazel-0060: You came by with an axe.
hazel-0061: Come back tomorrow. Bring the shovel, leave the axe, and wear that shirt again.
hazel-0062: Day four. Word's got round that someone is digging by the old hazel instead of cutting it down. The miller's daughter brings you lunch, and you walk her back as far as the footbridge.
hazel-0063: When you get back, a branch creaks overhead in a way that sounds very deliberate.
hazel-0064: The ferns say you walked the miller's daughter to the footbridge. That's fine. I'm sure no branch will fall on her. Fairly sure.
hazel-0065: A twig drops, very precisely, into your lunch.
hazel-0066: Her father came by too. You've got till the end of the month. Then he hires someone with a saw.
hazel-0067: So dig faster. I've started making plans for summer, and you're in most of them.
hazel-0068: She was being friendly. You're the one I come here for.
hazel-0069: I know. The ferns mentioned that too.
hazel-0070: Eat your lunch. She makes good bread, apparently. Nobody's ever walked me to a footbridge.
hazel-0071: You're not jealous? Your leaves are going red.
hazel-0074: Dig your trench. And stop looking at my leaves.
hazel-0075: The trench reaches the river on the night of a storm. Water floods into the new channel, and the whole tree shudders.
hazel-0076: It's fine. It's the roots letting go of the old wall. They've held it forty years. They're making a fuss.
hazel-0077: You sit with your back against the trunk while it rains. Every so often she makes a small sound, and you put your hand flat on the bark.
hazel-0078: You didn't have to stay. You're soaked. You'll get ill, and then I'll have to look after you, and I've no idea how.
hazel-0079: Talk to me. About anything. What did you have for breakfast?
hazel-0080: Tell me about the grove when it was a forest.
hazel-0081: There were wolves. And a family of woodcutters who sang while they worked. I liked them, even though they were woodcutters.
hazel-0082: She talks until the storm passes. You fall asleep against her before she's finished, and she doesn't seem to mind.
hazel-0083: You're still warm. I'll keep you.
hazel-0084: I'll list everyone in town you'd like to drop a branch on.
hazel-0085: Start with the baker. He leans on me when he smokes.
hazel-0086: She laughs, and a shower of rainwater falls off her leaves onto your head.
hazel-0087: Then the miller. Then the miller again.
hazel-0088: By the end of the month the old wall has stopped cracking. The new millrace runs clean, and Aldous Brock stands on the bank for a long time with his hat in his hands.

hazel-0090: Forty springs he's sent people with axes. That's the first time he's ever touched me.

hazel-0092: I can go as far as my roots do. Thanks to someone, that's quite far now. Far enough to follow you home, if I felt like it.
hazel-0093: The moss on the east side is softer than it looks. I've been meaning to mention that for about a week.
hazel-0094: Stay tonight. I'll keep the rain off. I'm not promising anything else.
hazel-0096: The moss on the east side is softer than it looks. Above you her branches have spread and knitted together, and the first rain ticks against the leaves without coming through.
hazel-0097: Two hundred years people have walked past this tree. Not one of them ever lay down under it. Shift over, you're on a root.
hazel-0098: The badgers are watching. I told them to go away. Nobody in this grove listens to me.
hazel-0099: Her hands are warm now. They were cold the first time you touched the bark. She sees you notice.
hazel-0100: That's you. You did that. A month of you leaning on me with your sleeves rolled up.
hazel-0101: She pulls you down by your shirt. Her hair falls round you both, gold at the top and green at the ends, and it smells of rain.
hazel-0102: Tell me if I get this wrong. I've read about it in exactly one book, and a woodcutter dropped it here before the mill was built.
hazel-0103: Slowly. I've had two hundred years of nothing happening. I'd like this to take a while.

hazel-0105: Don't look at the leaves. They're being ridiculous.
hazel-0106: And don't tell the ferns. They'll want details.
hazel-0107: Sleep. I'll wake you if the miller comes. I might not.
hazel-0108: It rains all night. None of it reaches you.

hazel-0112: Two hundred years, and nobody told me it could feel like that. I'd like it noted that I'm saying this very calmly.

hazel-0117: That one's fine. That one's fine. Not that one. I mean it. Don't.

hazel-0120: Go on, then. What are you planting? It'll outlast both of us. Well. It'll outlast you.
hazel-0121: You say another hazel, so she isn't the only one.
hazel-0122: A neighbour. I've never had a neighbour.
ui-0009: Swap two gems next to each other to line up three or more of the same kind. Matched gems pop and score points; new ones fall in from the top.
ui-0011: Each chapter has a points goal and a number of moves. Reach the goal before your moves run out and the story carries on. There's no timer: take as long as you like.
ui-0013: Every girl has a favourite gem and one she dislikes (it's on her card in the roster). Matching her favourite fills the Charm ring faster.
ui-0015: Once you've cleared her first chapter, her card on the roster has a gift for her. Give it and her favourite gem shows up more often in all her chapters, for good.
ui-0017: Every match fills the Charm ring. When it's full you get a Charm Burst: +150 points.
ui-0019: Match 4 in a row to make a Rocket, which clears its row or column. Match 5, or an L or T shape, to make a Starburst. Swap a special gem to set it off; swap two together for a Mega Blast.
ui-0021: When falling gems make new matches on their own, that's a combo. Each link in the chain scores more than the last.
ui-0023: Dark, cracked shards cost you points when they're part of a match. The Hammer smashes one for free.
ui-0025: +3 Moves, the Hammer (smash any one gem) and Shuffle (new board) sit under the board. Buy them, and one-chapter boosts, in the Item Shop with the stars you earn.
ui-0027: After each chapter you pick a reply. A warm one starts her next chapter with bonus points; a teasing one costs a few, but she likes those too.
ui-0029: Running out still pays you a few stars. Try again, use +3 Moves, or visit the shop. Later chapters are hard without power-ups: short on stars, replay a chapter you've cleared from her card on the roster. Lose three times in a row and you can carry on with the story anyway.
ui-0031: Click, Space or Enter: next line. Hold Ctrl or press Skip: skip lines you've read. A or Auto: lines play on by themselves. L, Log or scroll up: read back. H: hide the text on full-screen pictures. Text speed is in Settings.
ui-0035: Stars — earned by clearing chapters, spent in the Item Shop and on gifts.
ui-0046: The full game has four stories: Hazel's, and three more women of Millbrook to meet in the worst way possible. Each has four chapters, her night scene and her ending.
